justifications.reason: `Assembly.GetName().Version?.ToString()` guards a null version. A compiled assembly always has one, so the null side cannot occur.

Defensive catch-all of ShutdownAsync, whose `finally` still completes the shutdown. Every step inside it either handles its own failures (cancel, close, timeouts: tested in shutdown_is_bounded and shutdown_closes_every_session_even_if_one_fails) or cannot throw; no input is known to reach this handler. It exists so that an unforeseen bug is logged instead of lost in an unobserved task.

justifications.match: using var process = Process.Start(info) ?? throw new FileNotFoundException(file);
justifications.reason: Process.Start returns null only when it reuses an already running process. With a new ProcessStartInfo for an executable file it starts a new process or throws, so the null side cannot occur.

Windows Credential Manager (CredReadW). Platform-specific: the Windows CI job runs it for real (credential_manager_windows, and the end-to-end test through Credential Manager) but is not instrumented, because the coverage tools run on Linux only. Off Windows the refusal is tested (credential_edges).

Handler for a state directory that exists but cannot be listed (permission denied, I/O error). A test that creates the directory has the right to list it, and running as root bypasses permission checks, so the failure cannot be provoked. The handler's answer is the safe one: nothing is dead, so nothing is ever swept.

justifications.match: return false; // exited while we looked
justifications.reason: A race: the process exits between GetProcessById and reading its StartTime. It cannot be produced on demand; the answer (not alive) is the same as for a process that was already gone, which is tested (instances_dead_ids).

justifications.match: return true; // cannot read its start time
justifications.reason: A process of another user whose start time cannot be read (Win32Exception). The test runs as the same user (or root, which can read every process), so it cannot be provoked. The answer is the safe one: not provably dead, so never swept.

PostgreSQL older than 14 has no client_connection_check_interval. CI servers are 14 or newer (PostgreSQL 17 in Docker, the runner's on Windows), so the branch needs a server version the project does not run.

A PostgreSQL server on Windows rejects any non-zero client_connection_check_interval. The Windows CI job takes this path (its backend_killed scenario reports it) but is not instrumented; on Linux the server accepts the value.

XACT_STATE() = -1 (an uncommittable transaction). SQL Server rolls such a transaction back at the end of the batch (error 3998), and the state is read between batches, so it is never -1 when read. Tried: a THROW under XACT_ABORT ON inside TRY dooms the transaction, and the next probe still sees none. The arm stays so a future server that keeps the transaction is reported as aborted, not active.

The commit refusal for an aborted transaction follows from the state above, which SQL Server never reports between batches (see XACT_STATE -1). PostgreSQL has the same refusal and it is tested there (tx_aborted_commit_refused).

query_start can be NULL only for a session that never ran a statement. Every dbbliss session runs statements while connecting (the interval setting and the sweep itself) before it can be killed, so its query_start is set.

state is NULL only for background workers, never for a client session, and the elapsed seconds are NULL for the same sessions as query_start (see above). The fallbacks in the message exist for a future server, not for any state seen.

pg_terminate_backend returns false when the session is already gone or not ours: a race between listing and ending it. Not provoked by a test; the answer is a different warning text, nothing is ended.

justifications.match: Could not end a session left by a dbbliss backend that was killed ({what}): {ex.
justifications.reason: Ending the session fails with a server error (for example a session owned by another role, which needs a second database role to provoke). Not tested; the handler turns the error into a warning and the connect goes on.

justifications.match: Could not check for sessions left by killed dbbliss backends
justifications.reason: Listing the sessions fails (a dropped connection or an unexpected column type). Not tested; the handler turns the error into a warning and the connect goes on, nothing is swept.
The -1 arm (an uncommittable transaction) is never taken: SQL Server rolls such a transaction back at the end of the batch, before the state is read (see the entry for -1 below).

justifications.match: Log.Warn($"could not remove the partial backup
justifications.reason: Cleanup of a partial file that fails (the file is locked, the folder is read-only) after the backup already failed or was cancelled: the original error is what the user needs and is thrown right after; the Warn only records that the cleanup failed. Needs a file the process may create but not delete, which the test user (root on a developer's container, an ordinary user in CI, Windows) does not give the same way everywhere.

justifications.match: catch (Exception ex) when (ex is InvalidOperationException or Win32Exception)
justifications.reason: Kill of a process that ended between the cancel and the kill: a race of a few microseconds that a test cannot provoke on purpose; the catch only makes it harmless.
Which executable name to look for depends on the operating system; the other side runs on the other platform's CI job (tools_are_found_where_they_are, cancel suite).
